segments.text: Robyn: Today, we're here with Margaret A. Neale.
She is the Adams Distinguished Professor
of Management Emerita at Stanford University's Graduate
School of Business.
Her bio is linked in the dashboard.
We have a lot of great, wonderful material here for you
today, and we might run over.
For the first time ever, I'm saying that.
Because I think it's important for everyone
to be able to stay on if they can.
If not, you're going to get the recording.
Stay on for Q&A. Please submit the questions.
I think you're going to have lots of things to ask.
Maggie, thanks so much for being here today with us.
And take it away.
MARGARET NEALE: Well, thanks, Robyn.
And thanks for joining me today.
I'm actually speaking from a hotel room
in Oregon, where I'm taking a little bit of a holiday.
But I will just tell you that there is a lot of content,
and I want to apologize in advance if it just
feels like a fire hose because there's so many things I
want to talk to you about.
And so the first thing I want to do,
because my area is negotiation, and the courses that I teach
are in negotiation.
So one of the things I want you to think about
is that one of the challenges we face and the way people think
about negotiation is they think about it as a battle.
And oftentimes, even more constraining,
they think about it as an activity
that they engage in if they were negotiating a contract
or if they were negotiating a compensation plan
for new job or a promotion.
But it's so much broader than that.
But what happens is when people say the word negotiation,
the sense we get is that this is going to be a fight.
We're going to fight.
And so we look at negotiation as this process,
where I'm going to try to get stuff from you that you don't
want me to have, and I'm going to try to keep you
from getting my stuff.
And if that's how you think about negotiation,
you're doing yourself a disservice.
Because what happens when you take that mindset is that
becomes a filter through which you evaluate your counterpart.
And because they are the enemy, they are the other,
they are what's keeping you from getting more of what you want,
you're going to interpret their behaviors
in an adversarial and malevolent way.
And oftentimes, when you are in that negotiation mindset,
you begin to focus on single issues,
like a financial nature, like contracts, and compensation,
and things like that.
And you don't think broadly about what's possible.
And that's what I want to talk to you about today
is think about negotiation as much more than simply
figuring out a price, or a salary range, or a contract.
It's much more than that.
So I want you to broaden your definition
of what is negotiation.
And that is that negotiation is influence.
It's all about getting a decision
that meets your needs better and maybe the needs
of your counterparts as well.
So it's actually about improving a situation
in which you and your counterparts find yourselves.
So it's the process, where two or more
people decide what each is willing to give
and hopes to get in their interaction,
and through a process of mutual influence and persuasion.
Again, it's influence.
There's no command and control.
I can't force you to say yes.
But what I want to do is I want to exchange proposals and find
a solution that makes it easy for both of us to say yes.
Now, what that means is that in doing that,
I'm going to suggest a strategy that I think is really useful,
and that is to change your mindset from looking
at negotiations, these kinds of influence
attempts that you make when you don't
have command and control to collaborative problem solving.
Remember that negotiations are interdependent.
Influence is interdependent.
You and your counterpart must voluntarily
agree to the outcome.
And especially if you're negotiating
with folks who are either equal to or above you
in the organization, it's a voluntary process.
And it acknowledges that you don't have command and control.
So what you want to do is you want
to create a solution, where you are better off because there's
been some changes, or some things that you want,
or some new information.
You're better off than the status quo or your alternatives,
where your counterpart is better off because of those changes.
But certainly not worse off.
But here's the important point.
And this is number three.
You want to frame the proposals that you
make to them as solutions to a problem that you and they have.
It's about both a solution to a problem that they have.
Because one of the things that becomes really critical when
you're trying to get someone to move in a direction,
is you need to understand what their interests are,
what their preferences are, what their challenges are,
what their constraints are.
Now, it turns out this is actually a challenging process.
Because it turns out that, if you think you're negotiating,
then you get in this battle mentality.
So just set that aside and think about these kinds
of interactions as collaborative problem solving,
and then think about how can I help my counterpart
while helping myself be better.
So you need to create options here.
And that's really the-- you need to be creative.
And this is what's a challenge about this.
Because in order to embrace this perspective,
you've got to think about basically
what's important to your counterpart,
but also what's important to you.
And the creativity comes in merging those two
sets of interests, where you're able to find
a solution that where they think they're going to improve
and you know you're going to improve.
So that's the sweet spot.
But that takes planning and preparation.
And that takes creativity.
You can't just simply do kind of a off the top of your head knee
jerk.
You've got to prepare.
So if you take this perspective, you
can influence outcomes with your subordinates,
with your superiors, with your peers.
And you can improve the projects that you're
on by making them more effective given
the scenario, the environment, the situation that you're in.
But as you expand your opportunities here,
you really need to think carefully
about what it is that will make you first better off.
And so what I want you to think about here
is I want you to think about the goal.
The goal is not simply to get along.
The goal is not simply to acquiesce
if someone makes a demand of you to just say yes.
What the goal is to get a better outcome.
For example, an improved allocation
of scarce resources for you or your project,
a more workable solution or a better working relationship.
Those are all things that you can negotiate,
you can problem solve around.
And in doing so, you can improve your standing
in the organization, you're standing with your superiors,
you're standing with your subordinates.
So what you need to think about, and part of the planning
you need to think about is what are the boundaries that affect
what you're trying to achieve.
And so I'm going to give you three boundaries that you
need to think about.
And the first boundary is what happens
if you can't make these kinds of adjustments.
So what's your fallback position?
You really need to understand that alternative that is what
happens to you if perhaps you're given-- you're given a new--
a new aspect of your task or your project.
And there's nothing happens, but you just say yes.
So what does that look like for you?
And also, what you need to think about is--
a second point is, well, what's the worst thing
that you could be happy with?
What's that point, where you go from a situation you'd
like to say no to to one that you could say yes to?
So you want to think about where that tipping point is.
Because that tipping point is a really important position
for you to understand to know when you're going to--
you at least don't have to push as hard.
Because you've gotten above that point where you say,
I'm better off here.
But that's not where you want to stop.
Where you want to--
what you also want to think about,
and I think this is actually one of the most critical aspects
of these three boundaries, is what's a stretch goal?
So as you are preparing for this meeting with your superior,
or a peer, or even a subordinate,
what would a really good outcome look like for you given
the situation that you're in?
So you want to basically set that
set that aspiration in terms of where you are,
the experience that you have, your environment,
but what would be a really good outcome for you?
What kind of resources might you be able to garner?
What kind of outcomes might you be
able to achieve if you were able to get those resources that you
need or able to find the additional folks that you need,
or able to get more financial resources?
What might you be able to do to improve
the quality of the projects of which you are a part?
So I'm going to give you and suggest
that there are two routes that we can follow to improve
your negotiated outcomes, to improve your influence attempts
basically.
And I want to talk about number one,
is the use of justifications.
Explaining why you're doing what you're doing.
And with that comes the importance
of understanding the power of the ask.
And then we're going to talk about how
to avoid scope creep through the use of packaging.
So that's a really important one as well.
So let's get started on those two.
So the way I want to talk about influence through justifications
and the power of the ask is, I want
to demonstrate to you through the use
of a classic social psych experiment.
Now, when I say classic, I will readily
admit that this study was done decades ago.
In fact, I suspect this study was published before many of you
were born.
Doesn't mean it's wrong.
It just means we call it a classic now.
So here's the study.
Researchers were asked to go to organizations
and find the copy room.
Now, this study actually was conducted in 1977.
So yes, it is old.
And when the researchers found the copy room,
they were asked to wait until there
was a line at the copy machine.
And for those of you, you may have heard about this.
I certainly live this.
When I was a graduate student, when
I was an employee, and a pretty low status employee.
We would have to stand in line at the copy machine
making copies.
That was one of the jobs that I did a lot of.
Or you are trying to study for finals,
and you had to make copies of things,
and there was a copy machine in the library,
and you stood in line.
And so the question--
so the researchers went into these organizations
and found the room with the copy machine and waited.
And they waited until there was a line at the copy machine.
And then they went to the person who
was about to step up to make copies.
And basically, they were told by the study designer,
I want you to go in and see if you can get that person who's
about to step up to the copy machine
to let you cut in front of them, but you can only
use one of three possible strategies.
Here are the three strategies.
First is, we're going to do the simple ask.
May I use the copy machine?
OK.
The second strategy is, you're going
to ask to use the copy machine.
May I use the copy machine?
And then you're going to say a reasonable explanation for why
you're making this ask, may I use the copy machine.
Because I'm in a real rush.
And then the third strategy is make the ask,
but give a stupid justification.
May I use the copy machine because I need to make copies.
And so what then she said, is you
need to then tally how many people allow
you to step in front of them with each of these three
strategies.
OK, so that was the study.
So they went out into the organizations.
They found the copy machines.
Researchers got all this data, and then they
came back and analyzed it.
So let's see what they found.
So here's the first one.
First one is may I use the copy machine.
Now, this is just straightforward
asking for what they wanted.
Now, I want you to think for a minute.
And I want each of you, as you're
listening to me, to think about what's the problem--
what's the percentage of folks who think said yes.
Now, this is 1977.
In the US.
What percent of folks, when they were asked,
may I use the copy machine, said, sure,
and let people step in front of them?
Well, would it surprise you that the answer
was 60% of folks said yes.
And if it did, that's interesting, right.
Because most of us are surprised by that number.
We're surprised because we think that that's a real--
I mean, that's kind of a rude, weird thing.
Let me just cut in line.
May I use the copy machine.
But what this represents, and I think
this is so critical to your understanding of how
to be influential in your organizations,
this is the power of the ask.
These people were strangers.
They didn't have any kind of history with these people.
They didn't have a future with these people.
They just stepped up to them and said, may
I use the copy machine.
And 60% of folks said, yes.
We often avoid asking for what we want.
We avoid because we think people won't say yes to that.
We think they will be inconvenienced.
We think somehow they will think of us as weak.
But what I want to suggest to you
is that if you don't ask for what you want, how will others
know what it is you want?
If you don't ask for what you want,
then you're really basically forcing them to mind read.
And we, human beings, are terrible at this mind reading
thing.
But if you don't ask for what you want, who will?
And that's also important.
Because sometimes, your asks can change the entire conversation.
And what I think is even more surprising
for most folks is that people dramatically
underestimate how willing people are to accommodate.
You see, when you ask for something,
it turns out people want to grant those requests if they
can.
It gives the grantor a sense of agency,
a sense of having control and influence in their lives.
And so part of asking is really letting
people feel good about helping.
And there was actually while this study was done
in the 1970s, you'll see at the bottom left of the screen here
on my slides that there was a study that was recently
conducted that actually said people love to be able to help.
And they're to be able to-- they love being able to say,
I was able to do something.
And so one of the things that I've
done in my own personal life, as well as because
of the research and my own experience
since learning of this research, is
that I ask for what I want even when
I think it is really unlikely that they're going to say yes.
But I know if I don't ask, I already know the answer.
And if I do ask, I'm somewhat surprised
a lot of times about how willing people are to say, sure,
I can do that.
Or let me help you.
Or here's a way we can try to find a solution for that.
So I am a real proponent of the power of the ask.
All right.
So let's go to the second one.
And here is where we first use the justification.
So the question is, may I use the copy machine?
And then there's a justification of why I'm making this ask.
Because I'm in a real rush.
What do you think?
What did people do here?
What percent of folks said yes?
Well, 92%.
Now, I know that there are many of you
out there who are looking with a jaundiced eye at these results.
You're saying, these wouldn't hold in my culture,
in my company, or whatever.
People are not going to be either.
Only 60%.
We might have more people say yes or less
than we might be much, much, much lower.
These numbers are not sacred.
This 60% is not a sacred number.
What is important to see here is the delta
between asking alone and asking with a justification.
A 50% increase in compliance.
So part of what you want to think about here
is the importance of giving people an explanation for why
you're doing what you're doing.
A simple request is good.
It's important.
It's a great first step.
But I'm also going to suggest that it's
really critical for you to actually explain why
you're doing what you're doing.
And I'm a real proponent of this.
I tell people the thinking process underlying my position,
the things I'm hoping to achieve,
why I'm doing what I'm doing.
And I think that kind of transparency
actually enhances people's willingness
to accommodate your requests.
OK, let's go to the third one.
Now, this is kind of crazy, right.
This is like, may I use the copy machine?
Because I need to make copies.
Seriously, everybody in line needs to make copies.
But what percent of people here do you think said yes?
Well, this may surprise you.
Because actually, the number was 91%.
So there's not a whole lot of difference between--
in this situation between the justification
that's reasonable and a justification
that's just nonsense.
But if you don't believe these numbers,
think about your experience in the TSA line.
Have you ever been in a TSA line,
or have you been that person in the TSA line
who was late and goes running up to the line and says,
excuse me, excuse me, can I cut in line?
I need to make a flight.
Well, that's the same thing.
We're all in this line to make a flight.
Because today is Tuesday, and I'm here to fly.
I'm not here to just stand in line at the airport
because that's what I do.
No.
But what happens is, what appears to happen,
what the researchers have found is
that people will hear the request,
may I use the copy machine?
May I cut in line because--
and then they stop listening.
Because
They've already made the decision.
You see, these kinds of decisions.
Cutting in front-- cutting in line in the copy machine,
cutting in line in the TSA line, these are not
mission critical decisions.
And so what happens is people are like-- they've already
made the decision.
They're not going to engage that very costly, cognitive resources
in order to accommodate thinking about well, what
did they just say?
Make copies?
Well, we're all here to do that.
No, it's not worth it.
You've already decided, and then you move on.
Now, it turns out that justifications, sometimes
their mere presence in, especially
in trivial kinds of decisions, are
more powerful than the justification that you use.
But most of us are thinking about justifications
when we have decisions that are actually
going to be scrutinized, people are going to pay attention.
And so when that's the case, you need
to have more objective justifications.
You need to explain why.
And explaining why can mitigate your counterpart's resistance
to behaviors they're not expecting from you.
Explaining why helps.
And the reason it helps is because it provides the story
that you want to tell.
It gives them a narrative.
They don't have to make it up.
You're telling them why you're doing what you're doing.
And that's probably a whole lot more appropriate
story or narrative than the one they might come up
with on their own.
Now, second, avoiding scope creep
through the power of the package.
All right.
So turns out that oftentimes, when we're trying to enlarge
or trying to improve the quality of the decisions
and how we make them, we go by focusing a single issue
at a time.
I'm concerned I don't have enough marketing budget.
Let's talk about the marketing budget.
I'm concerned that my resources here,
in terms of my support staff, are not the quality that I need,
or I'm concerned that I'm not getting
the time on the computers that I need.
Whatever it is.
But we do it one at a time.
So what I want you to think about
is to think about creating value requires
that we think about these issues as a package.
Rather than engaging each issue by itself,
which is kind of a yes or a no issue, a win or a lose issue,
you want to think about multiple issues considered
simultaneously.
So you want to have a package.
Here's the package of resources that we
can craft that can help me improve
the project in terms of its performance
or in terms of its timeliness.
You might be able to craft that prep package,
but that requires that you understand
what's important to you in that, but also what's
important to your counterpart.
And what you're looking for are ways
that aren't very costly to you, that
are beneficial to your counterpart,
and ways that are not very costly to them,
that are beneficial to you.
And part of what we want to try to find
is that sweet spot, where you can make those trades.
But you need multiple issues within your package
to be able to make those trades.
That means you need to set priorities.
And what you're looking for are those asymmetries.
What's more important to you, less important to them.
What's less important to them and more important to you.
Those are the easy ones.
And then what you want to do is you
want to make a proposal that incorporates all of these.
Because what that does is it allows
you to identify and perhaps extract additional resources
to if you're getting that scope creep,
it's not just the frog in the boiling water
kind of thing or frog in the hot water that boils.
Eventually, it kind of dies.
But what happens is, is that you,
then as the scope of the project enlarges,
so do the resources associated with that project.
And so part of it is understanding
that we can have that negotiation,
we can have that conversation, and in fact get more resources
as the project requires them, rather than just simply going
along and sitting in that hot water as it gets hotter,
and hotter, and hotter.
So you shouldn't be afraid to add issues and be
creative about that because you want
to be expansive in the number of issues
that you bring to the table, because that
allows more of this opportunity for making trades.
Now, as you bring more issues to the table,
the interaction becomes more complex.
Absolutely.
And sometimes, it's so complex that people
begin making mistakes, and you get too much--
there's too much cognitive demand on it.
If your contracts are too complex,
it's really hard to keep them all in your head, all the issues
all at once.
So what you need to do is think about this theoretically
and make it smaller.
So you may not have all the issues in a particular package.
We call it a chunk.
So form chunks three issues at a time.
Maybe we can all deal with three issues at a time.
And think about that chunk.
And if you have lots of other issues,
think about that negotiation.
Think about that chunk.
Put it aside.
Once you've got it agreed to, don't take it off the table.
Put it aside.
The reason I'm telling you not to take it off the table
is because you've got lots of other chunks to agree to.
Once you got all the chunks agreed to,
then put it all back together, and make sure it makes sense.
Because time moves on, the environments change.
And if we've learned nothing from COVID, what we should learn
is we don't predict the future very well.
So you want to make sure that by the time you
finish the whole negotiation, everything still makes sense.
So here are the five tips we talked about in the first slide.
First is consider expanding your perspective on negotiation
from negotiation as battle to negotiation
as collaborative problem solving.
Know what your goal is and what you can and can't
accommodate in the interaction before you engage with it.
Understand the environment in which you're a part.
Leverage the power of the ask.
Ask for what you want.
And if there's nothing else you take from this little time
together, this is an important-- this is the important lesson.
Ask, ask, ask.
And let me just add to that.
Use justifications.
Explain to people why you are doing what you are doing.
Give them an alternative narrative.
That's the narrative you want them
to have as opposed to the narrative that they create.
And finally, package.
Multi issues are your friend.
This is the way you can create value.
And when you do that, you may find yourselves
being able to not only create more value,
but claim a bigger share of that pie
in terms of your status, your efficacy, your efficiency
in the organization, and the way in which you are perceived
by your workers, your counterparts,
and your superiors.
Now, if you want to know more, a couple of things
I'm going to suggest.
If you haven't read Robert Cialdini's book on Influence,
this one-- the 2009 was the last revision of his book
that he did before he went and retired emeritus.
I'd strongly recommend that you read this book.
This is an amazing-- he's done so much
research about influence, and he's got some great stories,
and he's an amazing writer.
So do that.
I think this next book is really good too.
It happens to be my book.
Getting more of what you want.
How the secrets of economics and psychology can help you
negotiate anything in business and in life.
And then also, there's a website associated with the book called
gettingmoreofwhatyouwant.com, which has more articles,
it has podcasts, it has video clips, it has articles
that I've written.
My colleague and I are there in video.
All that's up there.
You're welcome to peruse it.
And with that, I'm going to turn it back over to Robin.
Robyn: Maggie, thanks so much for that.
Every time you share your insights,
I always learn something more.
So thank you so much.
Everyone, we have a couple of questions that have come in.
I'm going to try to put them in different pieces,
and I'm going to put them together
in a more robust question.
While we're talking here, in the dashboard
is linked Maggie's course, getting more of what you want.
So you can see that there.
You can see her bio there.
We are at 9:30 right now, but we're going to stay on a couple
extra minutes and answer some questions.
Maggie, I really appreciated and it
seems like other people really appreciated
about what you said about the power of the ask.
You don't ask, you already know the answer
to it, which is going to be no because you
haven't asked the question.
Something that people are struggling with
and wonder how you handle this.
So you said in your personal life,
you've really learned the power of the ask.
How do you balance--
because I think that this is common amongst people.
How do you balance negotiating against yourself?
For example, the power of the ask.
Let's say you're leading a project.
You're leading a team.
Your hands a month ago, and you heard
from senior leadership about how tight things are,
and this, and that.
Now, you want to ask for what your project needs,
but also you're really wondering,
how is this ask going to go up against what I already going on
in the organization?
Am I going to make people mad?
Am I going to cross a line and make bring them to the point of,
I don't even know why this person is asking this?
Could you speak to that?
MARGARET NEALE: Sure.
And that requires you focusing on that aspect
of collaborative problem solving, which
is what are the interests of your counterpart
and what are the constraints they face.
That doesn't mean you shouldn't ask.
Because I can tell you, I have been
in so many situations in my life where people said oh, there's
no opportunity here.
Well, OK, maybe there's not generally opportunities,
but there are always, for good enough ideas,
for enough sort of insight and sort of creativity,
there are ways people find resources.
But again, it's up to you to be creative in that,
to understand your counterpart and to understand where
the opportunities that exist.
And so this is what I tell my students all the time.
And they often talk to me about, compensation, negotiation,
compensation plans.
And they're like, I want more money.
And I said, well, more money is good.
Absolutely.
Maybe there's some constraints there.
But when you ask for other things, other resources that
can help the organization or can help
you do a better-- you make a better
contribution to the organization,
people are going to listen.
They're going to consider that.
And while this is what the other benefit of a package is.
While you may not get everything,
you're probably not going to get zero.
You're probably going to get something.
So the point is you need to ask and realize that you
need to figure out how to ask.
And you have to ask in a way that says to the person,
I care about this organization, I care about my group,
I care about the project, and I want to make it better.
And here's what we can do to make this better.
Robyn: I think that's great.
So being collaborative, being open, and letting them know,
hey, I'm aware--
I'm aware a month ago, we had this all hands meeting,
and things are tight.
Here's why this is important.
And then as you said, bring in those justifications.
MARGARET NEALE: Right
Robyn: OK.
The other questions that seem to be bubbling up
are around packaging.
Because I think like me, like other people,
it's so much more linear to think of one at a time,
but it doesn't really serve our purpose.
So the packaging.
How can we, as individuals, get better at packaging?
Are we writing it down?
Are we boiling it down?
We heard that money was a big constraint.
So then we're upleveling something.
How do you get better at that other
than getting some part of it is in your plan right away?
MARGARET NEALE: Yeah.
Part of it is in your planning.
Your planning process before you even begin the conversation.
So you should be in there.
And that's what the creativity is around.
Think expansively about what resources
are available in the organization
or could be available in the organization.
You don't need to limit yourself to the obvious stuff.
What could be available, what's creative,
out of the box thinking and say, OK, here
are the resources that I would need in order
to be able to try that out.
Here are the resources that might
be very important for that.
So again, we're setting priorities, right.
This is a really important resource.
This is a resource that would be useful.
Maybe this is a resource that would be-- well,
if we went this way, then I could do the following six
things.
So you look at that before you even begin the conversation.
And you say to yourself, what's out there that's
possible that would help me do the job I need to do?
And that what's out there that's possible to help me do the job
I need to do?
Depends on the job you need to do.
Depends on where the pain points are,
and how you might be able to pivot,
and not basically experience those pain points directly
or perhaps find a way to cure the pain,
to find a way that makes the pain go away.
